text.en: Asha watched a pond dry up in summer and fill again in the rains. "Water moves in cycles," she said.

The biosphere is the part of Earth where life exists. Matter moves in biogeochemical cycles. The water or hydrological cycle is the continuous movement of water on Earth, and transpiration puts water vapour into the air. In the nitrogen cycle, decomposers return nitrogen from organic remains as ammonium. In nitrification, certain microorganisms convert ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate.
An adaptation is a feature that helps an organism live in its surroundings. Hydrophytes live in water, xerophytes in dry places and mesophytes in moderate conditions. Animals also have adaptations, such as those of the earthworm.
Water conservation saves water, as in farm ponds, and recycling treats wastewater for reuse. The IUCN, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, works for the protection of nature.

The biosphere includes living organisms and the parts of land, water and air where they live. An exchange between those parts can carry matter from one place to another.

board.text: Life interacts with air, land and water

text.en: Sunlight can provide energy for water at a pond surface to evaporate. The water changes from liquid to vapour, and the vapour enters the air.
A plant also releases water vapour, mainly from its leaves. This process is called transpiration. Both transpiration and evaporation add water vapour to the air.
When moist air cools, some water vapour condenses into liquid droplets. Many such droplets can contribute to a cloud.
Rain returns water to the land and oceans. Snow is another form of precipitation. The state and route can differ while the water remains part of the cycle.

board.text: Precipitation can be rain or snow

text.en: Water running over the ground can reach streams and ponds. Some water instead passes into spaces between soil particles and rock. That process is infiltration.

board.text: Runoff: over the ground · infiltration: into the ground

text.en: An open patch of soil can let some rain soak in. A paved area often sends more water over the surface. The amount also depends on slope, ground cover and the rainfall.
Plants and animals need nitrogen in molecules such as proteins. Most plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly, so the form in which nitrogen reaches the roots matters.

board.text: Soil nitrogen forms can be taken up by roots

text.en: Nitrogen fixation is one route from atmospheric nitrogen to forms that can enter living systems. Soil nitrogen then passes through plants, animals and decomposing remains.

board.text: Fixation links atmospheric and biologically available nitrogen

text.en: Decomposition returns material to soil. Nitrification changes the form of some soil nitrogen. Denitrification returns some nitrogen to the atmosphere.

board.text: Nitrogen moves between atmosphere, soil and organisms

text.en: Follow carbon dioxide from the air into a green leaf. Photosynthesis can incorporate the carbon into sugars. Carbon can then pass along a food chain.

board.text: Photosynthesis moves carbon from air into living matter

text.en: Respiration and decomposition return some carbon to the environment. Combustion can also return carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

board.text: Several processes return carbon to the air

text.en: Water, carbon and nitrogen can each move through a living organism. The three cycles describe different materials. Compare what is moving at each arrow.

board.text: Identify the material before tracing a cycle

text.en: A floating plant can have air spaces that help parts stay near the surface. This is one example of a feature that suits a plant living in water.

board.text: Hydrophytes live in or around water

text.en: A cactus can store water in its thick stem. In many cacti, spines take the place of broad leaves, which reduces the surface from which water can be lost.
Many familiar land plants grow in conditions that are neither extremely wet nor extremely dry. The term mesophyte describes plants of such moderate conditions.
A bat can send out sound pulses and use returning echoes to locate objects. That feature links an animal’s sense of its surroundings with how it navigates.
An earthworm’s long flexible body helps it move through soil. Its small bristles can grip the ground while body muscles change its shape.
A farm pond can collect rain runoff for later use, such as irrigation. Consider where the rain comes from and when the stored water might be needed.

board.text: Farm pond stores some runoff for later

text.en: Wastewater can be treated for suitable uses. Landscape irrigation is an example when the water meets the required quality. Whether it looks clear does not tell us whether it is suitable.

board.text: Recycled-water use depends on treatment quality

text.en: The IUCN Red List uses published criteria to describe extinction risk for species. Its categories help people compare evidence about different species and plan conservation priorities.
Choose a water conservation idea for a school map. Explain which flow or use would change, then name an observation that could show whether the idea helped.

board.text: Propose a change and decide what to measure

problem.en: After rain, water flows quickly from a school roof past an open garden. Describe one way to collect some water for a suitable later use and explain the change in its route.

text.en: Trace water from the roof to a collection point.

why.en: Collecting part of the runoff keeps it from immediately flowing away.

text.en: Identify a suitable use such as watering the garden.

why.en: It can reduce the need for other irrigation water when the quality suits that use.

prompt.en: A friend says Nitrogen cannot be reused. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Bacteria change it between forms so it can be reused.
